title: Languages, logic and proof
subtitle: The vocabulary everything else is built on: strings, languages, and how to be sure a claim is true.

alpha.title: Alphabets, strings and languages
alpha.body: An alphabet Σ is a finite set of symbols, e.g. {0, 1}. A string is a finite sequence of them; ε is the empty string and Σ* the set of all strings. A language is any subset of Σ* — for example “all binary strings ending in 01”. The whole subject asks: how complicated a machine is needed to recognise a given language?
alpha.steps: Over Σ = {0, 1} how many strings have length exactly 3? Two choices for each of three positions.

ops.title: Operations on languages
ops.body: From languages L and M: union L ∪ M, concatenation LM (a string of L followed by one of M) and the Kleene star L* (zero or more strings of L joined). If L = {a, b} then L* contains ε, a, b, aa, ab, … — every string over {a, b}.

logic.title: Propositional logic and inference
logic.body: Statements combine with ¬ (not), ∧ (and), ∨ (or), → (implies), ↔ (iff). Key rules: modus ponens (from P and P → Q, conclude Q), modus tollens (from ¬Q and P → Q, conclude ¬P). De Morgan: ¬(P ∧ Q) = ¬P ∨ ¬Q. Predicate logic adds ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists).
logic.steps: Premises: “if it rains the match is cancelled” (R → C) and “the match was not cancelled” (¬C). Modus tollens gives ¬R.

proof.title: Proof techniques
proof.body: Direct proof; contradiction (assume the opposite and derive an absurdity — e.g. √2 is irrational); induction (prove a base case and that n ⇒ n+1); the pigeonhole principle (n+1 pigeons in n holes: some hole has two — the engine behind the pumping lemma); diagonalisation (build an object that differs from the i-th item in the i-th place — proves the reals are uncountable and the halting problem undecidable).
proof.steps: Prove 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2 by induction. Base n = 1: 1 = 1·2/2 ✓. Step: assume it for n; adding n+1 gives n(n+1)/2 + (n+1) = (n+1)(n+2)/2, the formula for n+1.

hier.title: The road ahead: the Chomsky hierarchy
hier.body: Four classes of language, each needing a stronger machine: regular (finite automaton) ⊂ context-free (pushdown automaton) ⊂ context-sensitive (linear-bounded automaton) ⊂ recursively enumerable (Turing machine). The rest of the course climbs this ladder.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• A language is a set of strings over an alphabet; ∪, concatenation and * build new ones.
  • Proofs: direct, contradiction, induction, pigeonhole, diagonalisation.
